1G (Number Theory)

Words: 168 Articles: 5

Solution

Words: 37
1G OurBigBook.com
For an odd prime number p and an integer n not divisible by p, the Legendre symbol χ(n)=(n/p) is 1 if n is a quadratic residue modulo p, and −1 otherwise. One may extend it by χ(n)=0 when p∣n.

i

Words: 102 Articles: 1
1G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 102
i OurBigBook.com
Put h=(p−1)/2. The nonzero quadratic residues in the finite field Fp​ form a subgroup of size h: the group homomorphism x↦x2 has kernel {1,−1}. Each square satisfies uh=1 by Fermat's little theorem. Since a nonzero polynomial of degree h has at most h roots of a polynomial, these are all the roots of Xh−1. For any other nonzero u, Fermat's theorem gives (uh)2=1, so uh=−1. Thus Euler's criterion follows, and multiplication gives
χ(mn)≡(mn)h=mhnh≡χ(m)χ(n)(modp).
(1)
Both sides are 1 or −1, which are distinct modulo the odd prime number p, so χ(mn)=χ(m)χ(n). Taking n=−1 in Euler's criterion gives χ(−1)=(−1)(p−1)/2, which is 1 for p≡1(mod4) and −1 for p≡3(mod4).

ii

Words: 29 Articles: 1
1G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 29
ii OurBigBook.com
Euler's criterion gives χ(−1)=(−1)(p−1)/2=1 in this case. There are equally many nonzero quadratic residues and quadratic nonresidues, so ∑n=1p−1​χ(n)=0. Replacing n by p−n and using the multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol gives
S=∑n=1p−1​(p−n)χ(p−n)=p∑n=1p−1​χ(n)−S=−S.
(2)
Consequently S=0​.

3F (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 117 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 117
3F OurBigBook.com
Let v=T(0) and B(x)=T(x)−v. The Euclidean isometry B fixes the origin and preserves norms. The polarization identity therefore gives ⟨Bx,By⟩=⟨x,y⟩. In particular, Be1​,Be2​ are an orthonormal basis. The coefficients of Bx in this basis are ⟨Bx,Bej​⟩=xj​, so Bx=x1​Be1​+x2​Be2​. Thus B is a linear map represented by an orthogonal matrix, and T(x)=Bx+v. Conversely, every such map preserves distances because ∥B(x−y)∥=∥x−y∥.
When detB=−1, the real eigenvalues of the two-dimensional orthogonal matrix are 1,−1. Choose corresponding unit eigenvectors e,n, and write v=ae+bn. In these coordinates T(s,t)=(s+a,−t+b). This is reflection in the line t=b/2, followed by translation ae along that line. It is a Euclidean reflection if a=0, and a glide reflection if a=0.

4H (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 176 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 176
4H OurBigBook.com
Take the parity-check matrix
H=​001​010​011​100​101​110​111​​
(5)
over F2​. Its columns are all the nonzero vectors of F23​. The Hamming code is C=kerH. Since H has rank three, C is a binary linear code of length seven and dimension four. No nonzero codeword has weight one or two, since no column is zero and no two columns coincide. Columns u,v,u+v give a codeword of weight three, so C has parameters [7,4,3].
For a received vector w=c+e, its syndrome is Hw=He. A single error in position j gives exactly column j of H, so the syndrome identifies that position uniquely; zero syndrome means no error under the one-error assumption. The radius-one Hamming balls around the 16 codewords are disjoint and have total size 16(1+7)=128=27, so this is also a perfect code.
There are (27​)/3=7 weight-three codewords: every pair of columns determines the third, and each triple is counted three times. The all-ones vector is a codeword because the column sum is zero, so complementation gives seven weight-four codewords. Together with zero and the all-ones vector these account for all sixteen. The weight enumerator is therefore
WC​(z)=1+7z3+7z4+z7​.
(6)

5J (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 153 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 153
5J OurBigBook.com
A maximum-likelihood estimator maximizes the likelihood as a function of the parameter for the observed data. Under the usual regularity conditions, a scalar maximum-likelihood estimator satisfies n​(θ^−θ)⇒N(0,I1​(θ)−1), where I1​ is the Fisher information in one observation.
For a Poisson distribution with θ>0, the log-likelihood is ℓ(θ)=∑j​Yj​logθ−nθ−∑j​log(Yj​!). Solving ℓ′(θ)=0 gives θ^=Yˉ​. Its expectation is θ and its variance is θ/n. If all observations are zero, the maximum over θ≥0 occurs at zero; over θ>0 this is a boundary supremum. The one-observation score function is Y/θ−1, so I1​(θ)=Var(Y)/θ2=1/θ and the asymptotic variance of n​(Yˉ−θ) is θ.
For n≥2, let S=(n−1)−1∑j​(Yj​−Yˉ)2. The identity
∑j​(Yj​−Yˉ)2=∑j​(Yj​−θ)2−n(Yˉ−θ)2
(7)
gives ES=(nθ−θ)/(n−1)=θ, so S is another unbiased estimator. However, the total score function has variance n/θ. For any regular unbiased estimator T, differentiating Eθ​T=θ gives Cov(T,ℓ′)=1, so the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality yields Var(T)≥θ/n. The sample mean attains this Cramér-Rao bound exactly. There is no variance advantage in preferring S to Yˉ.

6A (Mathematical Biology)

Solution

Words: 157
6A OurBigBook.com
Write f(u)=au2/(b2+u2), with b>0. Besides zero, the fixed points satisfy u2−au+b2=0. If a2>4b2, they are
u±​=2a±a2−4b2​​​.
(8)
The derivative is f′(u)=2ab2u/(b2+u2)2. At a positive fixed point, b2+u2=au, so f′(u)=2b2/(au)=2(1−u/a). Thus zero is attracting, u−​ is repelling because f′(u−​)>1, and u+​ is attracting because 0<f′(u+​)<1.
Moreover,
f(u)−u=−b2+u2u(u−u−​)(u−u+​)​.
(9)
For 0<u0​<u−​ the iterates strictly decrease and stay positive. Their limit is a fixed point below u−​, hence zero. For u−​<u0​<u+​ the iterates increase towards u+​; for u0​>u+​ they decrease towards u+​. Monotonicity of f prevents crossing the limiting fixed point. u−​ is the extinction threshold. The cobweb plot illustrates these alternatives.
For a2<4b2 there are no positive fixed points, and f(u)<u for every u>0, so all populations tend to zero. At a2=4b2, the positive fixed point a/2 is semistable: initial populations below it tend to zero, and those above it decrease towards it. This is a saddle-node bifurcation in the discrete dynamics.

7D (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 242 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 242
7D OurBigBook.com
The only equilibrium point is (0,0). Its Jacobian matrix is (−μ−1​10​), with characteristic polynomial λ2+μλ+1. For μ>0 both eigenvalues have negative real parts, so the origin is locally asymptotically stable.
Use the Lyapunov function V=(x2+y2)/2. Along a solution,
V˙=xx˙+yy˙​=μx2(x2/3−1).
(10)
A Lyapunov function is positive away from the equilibrium and nonincreasing along trajectories; its sufficiently small sublevel sets prove stability. Asymptotic stability additionally means nearby trajectories converge to the equilibrium. The basin of attraction is the set of initial states whose forward solutions exist for all positive time and converge to it. Every closed disc of radius at most 3​ is positively invariant, since V˙≤0 there. The LaSalle invariance principle says that a solution in a compact positively invariant set where V˙≤0 approaches the largest invariant subset of {V˙=0}. Here that subset is only the origin: on x=0, remaining on the line would require y=0; the isolated points x=±3​,y=0 on the outer disc do not remain there because y˙​=−x=0. Hence the closed disc x2+y2≤3 lies in the basin of attraction.
This estimate does not assert that the basin is exactly that disc, or the whole plane. For example, choose R so large that R2≥6(μ+1)/μ and R2>3(μ+2)/μ. The region x≥R, y≥−x is positively invariant: on x=R one has x˙>0, and on y=−x one has (x+y)⋅=μx3/3−(μ+2)x>0. Within it x˙≥μx3/6, which forces finite-time escape. Thus the attraction is genuinely local. The Lyapunov function gives a rigorous sufficient domain for attraction without identifying its entire boundary.

The photon number density is obtained by integrating the Planck photon distribution. With x=hν/(kT),
n=c38π​∫0∞​ehν/(kT)−1ν2dν​=αc3h38πk3​∫0∞​ex−1x2​dx​​T3.
(15)
The integral converges, since its integrand is of order x near zero and decays exponentially at infinity. Hence n=αT3, with α independent of temperature.
For equilibrium radiation undergoing adiabatic expansion, the total entropy in a comoving volume is constant. Since the entropy density is βT3, this means βT3V is constant. A comoving volume scales as the cube of the scale factor, so
T∝V−1/3∝a−1​.
(16)
This agrees with the cosmological redshift of each photon frequency. The conclusion uses entropy conservation during the expansion.

i OurBigBook.com
The planar Brouwer fixed-point theorem states that every continuous map from a closed disc to itself has a fixed point.

ii

Words: 111 Articles: 1
11F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 111
ii OurBigBook.com
Suppose first that a retraction R:D→C exists. The continuous map p↦−R(p) takes D to itself, so the Brouwer fixed-point theorem gives p=−R(p). Such p lies on C, where R(p)=p, contradicting p=−p.
Conversely, suppose a continuous map T:D→D has no fixed point. For each p, follow the ray from T(p) through p to its last intersection with C. This defines a retraction. More explicitly, put a=p−T(p)=0 and set
R(p)=T(p)+t(p)a,t(p)=∣a∣2−T(p)⋅a+(T(p)⋅a)2+(1−∣T(p)∣2)∣a∣2​​.
(17)
The positive-root formula is continuous, t(p)≥1, and R(p) is on the unit circle. If p∈C, the last intersection is p itself, so R(p)=p. Thus the nonexistence of a retraction rules out a fixed-point-free T, proving the equivalence.

Fix z with ∣z∣<1−ε, and let Π(w)=w/max(1,∣w∣) be radial projection to the closed disc. The continuous map p↦Π(p−G(p)+z) has a fixed point p by the Brouwer fixed-point theorem. On the boundary, ∣p−G(p)+z∣<ε+∣z∣<1, so its image under Π is interior and cannot equal the boundary point p. Therefore p∈B. An interior fixed point of this projection must satisfy p−G(p)+z=p, because points outside the disc project to its boundary. Thus G(p)=z. Every z∈B1−ε​(0) belongs to G(B).

12H OurBigBook.com
The Vandermonde determinant is
detV(x0​,…,xr−1​)=0≤i<j<r∏​(xj​−xi​)​.
(18)
Indeed, the determinant is an alternating polynomial, hence divisible by every xj​−xi​. Both sides have degree r(r−1)/2, and comparison of the coefficient of x00​x11​⋯xr−1r−1​ gives constant one. This is an identity over the integers, so reducing its coefficients modulo a prime number preserves it. For r>p, two residues coincide and the determinant vanishes. For r=p, choose all elements of Fp​ once to obtain a nonzero determinant.
For the ordering 0,1,…,p−1, this determinant is D=∏j=1p−1​j!. If p is odd, put h=(p−1)/2. Wilson theorem gives j!(p−1−j)!=(−1)j+1. Pairing the factors with indices j=0,…,h−1 and p−1−j, and leaving h! unpaired, gives
D=(−1)h(h+1)/2h!.
(19)
Every distinct ordering changes the determinant by its permutation sign; repeated residues give zero. Thus the possible values are 0,±h! for odd p, and 0,1 for p=2.
Use Shamir's secret sharing: choose independent uniform a1​,…,ar−1​∈Fp​, and engrave the shares (xi​,P(xi​)), where P(X)=N+∑j=1r−1​aj​Xj and the xi​ are distinct nonzero field elements. We may take p>n; otherwise use a sufficiently large finite field extension and an agreed integer encoding. Any r shares determine P by polynomial interpolation and hence N=P(0). Given any r−1 shares and any proposed N, their equations in the coefficients have a unique solution: the coefficient matrix has determinant ∏i​xi​ times a nonzero Vandermonde determinant. Since the coefficients were uniform, the observed shares have the same distribution for every N. Thus they give no information about the secret.
For the fake, reduce its integers to field elements and first check that its abscissa is distinct and nonzero. Random collisions or a zero abscissa are immediately detectable and have probability O(n/p); the following conclusions concern the overwhelmingly likely distinct-abscissa case.
With r shares, there is always a unique degree-at-most-r−1 interpolating polynomial. If all shares are genuine it gives the correct secret. If one is fake, it normally gives the wrong secret, with probability 1−1/p conditional on a uniform fake ordinate, but the inconsistency is undetectable from those r shares. The data do not certify which case has occurred.
With r+1 shares, genuine shares are consistent with one such polynomial. A fake is inconsistent with probability 1−1/p, so it is usually detected as an inconsistency. However, omitting each of the r+1 shares in turn gives r+1 possible polynomials. If the data are inconsistent, their constant terms are distinct: two candidate polynomials with the same constant term agree at zero and at their r−1 common abscissae, hence agree identically, which would make all the data consistent. The secret is narrowed to r+1 possibilities, but the fake is not identified.
With r+2 shares, at least r+1 are genuine. There is a unique degree-at-most-r−1 polynomial agreeing with at least r+1 shares: two candidates would agree on at least r abscissae and hence coincide. Find it by deleting each share and checking consistency. The secret is recovered uniquely, and the fake is identified unless it happens to lie on the genuine polynomial, in which case it is harmless.

A matching in a graph from X to Y chooses one distinct neighbour in Y for each vertex of X. For a finite bipartite graph, the Hall marriage theorem states that such a matching exists if and only if ∣Γ(A)∣≥∣A∣ for every A⊆X. Necessity follows because the matched neighbours of A are distinct members of Γ(A).
For sufficiency use induction on ∣X∣, with the empty and one-vertex cases immediate. If some nonempty proper A satisfies ∣Γ(A)∣=∣A∣, the induced graph on A,Γ(A) satisfies Hall's condition. The remaining graph on X∖A,Y∖Γ(A) does too: for B⊆X∖A,
∣Γ(B)∖Γ(A)∣=∣Γ(A∪B)∣−∣Γ(A)∣≥∣B∣.
(31)
Inductively match both pieces and combine them. If no nonempty proper subset is tight, choose an edge xy and remove its endpoints. Every nonempty subset B of the remaining X is proper in the original X, so ∣Γ(B)∣≥∣B∣+1; removing y preserves Hall's condition. Match the remainder inductively and add xy. This proves the theorem without a flow or disjoint-path theorem.

A point of the surface is a germ of a branch obtained by analytic continuation of the original function. A representative analytic branch on a small disc gives a neighbourhood of germs, one at each centre in that disc. Projection to the centre is a complex coordinate chart; overlaps have identity transition maps. Complete continuation along every path gives a Riemann surface with an unramified covering map π to U. Lifting a closed path starting at each germ above P analytically continues that branch back to P, permuting the fibre. Reverse paths give inverse permutations, and concatenation gives their composition. This is the monodromy action of a covering space.
Write A=z2−1​, B=z2−4​. There are four branches (++),(+−),(−+),(−−), which are distinct: neither square root vanishes on U, and A2−B2=3 prevents A=±B. Small loops about either 1 or −1 change the sign of A only; loops about either 2 or −2 change the sign of B only. Label the four branches in the displayed order. The corresponding permutations are (13)(24) and (12)(34), respectively. Every loop in this punctured plane is generated up to homotopy by these puncture loops, so no other generators arise. The resulting monodromy group of a covering is
{1,(13)(24),(12)(34),(14)(23)}≅C2​×C2​​.
(42)
It acts transitively and regularly on the four branches.

A lambda-system contains the whole space and is closed under complements and countable disjoint unions. Let D be the smallest lambda-system containing a pi-system P. For A∈P, the family of B∈D with A∩B∈D is a lambda-system containing P, hence is all of D. Fixing B∈D and repeating the argument shows D is closed under intersections. A lambda-system closed under intersections is a sigma-algebra, so D=σ(P). This proves the pi-lambda theorem. If two probability measures agree on P, the sets on which they agree form a lambda-system; thus they agree on σ(P).
The nonnegative form of Fubini's theorem, also called Tonelli theorem, states that for a nonnegative product-measurable function on two sigma-finite measure spaces, the product integral equals either iterated integral, allowing the value infinity.
For Lebesgue measure on the plane, a bounded interval rectangle I×J has measure ∣I∣∣J∣. Its preimage under f is (λI)×(λ−1J), which has the same measure. Under g, its vertical slice at x∈I is J−sx, whose one-dimensional Lebesgue measure is ∣J∣ by translation invariance. Tonelli therefore gives μ(g−1(I×J))=∣I∣∣J∣. Horizontal slices likewise prove the equality for h. The interval rectangles form a generating pi-system. Sigma-finite measure uniqueness, obtained by the finite-measure pi-lambda argument on an increasing rectangular exhaustion, extends these equalities to all Borel sets. Completion extends them to all Lebesgue-measurable sets, since Borel null sets and their subsets remain null.
Writing λ2=c, matrix multiplication gives

Under the simple null, the probability integral transform makes Ui​=F(Xi​) independent uniform variables on [0,1]. Strict monotonicity and continuity identify the empirical distribution under this change of coordinates, so
Dn​=sup0≤u≤1​∣Gn​(u)−u∣.
(57)
Its null law is therefore independent of F.
For the composite null, the joint density is θ−n∏i​1{0≤xi​≤θ}​. Its parameter dependence is only through M=maxi​Xi​, proving sufficiency by the Fisher-Neyman factorization theorem; the larger statistic (J,M) is sufficient too. Ties have probability zero. For fixed j, the density of (J=j,M=ξ) is ξn−1/θn, 0<ξ<θ, because the other coordinates range independently over [0,ξ]. Dividing the joint density by this marginal gives conditional density
ξ−(n−1)∏i=j​1{0≤xi​≤ξ}​.
(58)
Thus the remaining observations are conditionally independent U[0,ξ].
For n≥2, discard the maximum and apply the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to the n−1 ratios Xi​/M, i=J, against U[0,1]. Use the ordinary null critical values for sample size n−1. Its conditional, hence unconditional, level is independent of θ. Keeping the fitted maximum and using the ordinary n-sample critical values would not have that justification.

Relative to a filtration (Fn​), a martingale is an adapted integrable process with E[Mn+1​∣Fn​]=Mn​; a supermartingale has the corresponding inequality ≤. A stopping time T has {T≤n}∈Fn​ for every n.
For T≤N, the pathwise identity
MT​=M0​+∑k=1N​1{T≥k}​(Mk​−Mk−1​)
(65)
has Fk−1​-measurable indicators. Conditioning each summand gives zero expected increment for a martingale, and a nonpositive one for a supermartingale. All terms are integrable because the sum is finite. Thus EMT​=EM0​ and EM^T​≤EM^0​, proving the requested inequality when their initial values agree.
A self-financing strategy holds πn​ shares during period n, chosen using information at time n−1. Its cash investment is Xn−1​−πn​Sn−1​, which earns the risk-free return. Hence
Xn​=πn​Sn​+(1+r)(Xn−1​−πn​Sn−1​)=(1+r)Xn−1​+πn​[Sn​−(1+r)Sn−1​].
(66)
Use the terminal condition V(N,x,s)=U(x) from the original PDF. Conditional on the current state and past, the next return has the law of ξ1​ and is independent of the past. Therefore the conditional expectation of V(n+1,Xn+1​,Sn+1​) for the chosen holding πn+1​ is at most its supremum over all holdings, namely V(n,Xn​,Sn​). Assuming the finite values and integrability implicit in this stochastic-control formulation, the value process is a supermartingale.
It follows that EU(XN​)≤V(0,X0​,S0​) for every admissible strategy. If the strategy π∗ makes this process a martingale, equality holds for it. π∗ attains the upper bound and is optimal. No existence of an optimizer or finiteness of an unconstrained supremum is being assumed without the stated admissibility conditions.

The Lax-Milgram theorem states that on a real Hilbert space, a bounded bilinear form a satisfying a(v,v)≥c∥v∥2 for some c>0 represents every bounded linear functional uniquely: there is a unique u with a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for all v.
The clamped trace conditions define a closed subspace H∂2​(Ω) of the Sobolev space H2(Ω). On it take a(u,v)=∫Ω​ΔuΔv and ℓ(v)=∫Ω​fv. Both are bounded by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. The Dirichlet elliptic regularity estimate on a smooth bounded domain gives ∥v∥H2​≤C∥Δv∥L2​ for v∈H2∩H01​, so a(v,v)≥C−2∥v∥H22​. The Lax-Milgram theorem now gives exactly one u satisfying
∫Ω​ΔuΔv=∫Ω​fv(v∈H∂2​(Ω)).
(67)
Testing with compactly supported smooth v and integrating by parts twice gives Δ2u=f in distributions; the two boundary conditions hold as traces by the space's definition. This is the unique weak clamped biharmonic solution.

Testing a weak Neumann Poisson problem with the constant function one gives ∫Ω​f=0, proving necessity. For sufficiency, use the closed Hilbert space of mean-zero H1 functions. The given Poincaré inequality makes ∥∇v∥L2​ an equivalent norm there. Set
a(u,v)=∫Ω​∇u⋅∇v,ℓ(v)=−∫Ω​fv.
(68)
The negative sign corresponds to Δu=f. Poincare's inequality gives boundedness of ℓ and coercivity of a. The Lax-Milgram theorem supplies a unique mean-zero solution. Every v∈H1 is the sum of its mean-zero part and a constant; since ∫f=0, the weak identity extends to every v∈H1. This is precisely the weak equation with zero normal derivative as its natural boundary condition. Existence and uniqueness in the mean-zero space hold exactly when fˉ​=0.

The rotation unitary operator is U(n,θ)=exp(−iθn⋅J/ℏ). A state with zero orbital angular momentum has a rotationally invariant orbital factor; a spinless j=0 state is wholly unchanged. Zero orbital angular momentum alone does not rule out a nontrivial rotation of intrinsic spin angular momentum.
For spin one-half, J=ℏσ/2. Direct multiplication of the Pauli matrices gives σi​σj​=δij​I+iϵijk​σk​. The antisymmetric part vanishes when contracted with ai​aj​, hence
(J⋅a)2=4ℏ2∣a∣2​I​.
(74)
For a=0, the operator has trace zero, so its eigenvalues are ±ℏ∣a∣/2; for a=0 both are zero. With unit n, the even and odd powers in the exponential give
U(n,θ)=Icos(θ/2)−in⋅σsin(θ/2).
(75)
Take n′=(sinθ,0,cosθ). The rotated state ∣m′⟩θ​=U(y,θ)∣m′⟩ satisfies (n′⋅J)∣m′⟩θ​=m′ℏ∣m′⟩θ​, because UJ3​U†=n′⋅J. By the Born rule, the probability of this outcome in the initial state ∣m⟩ is ∣θ​⟨m′∣m⟩∣2=∣⟨m∣U(y,θ)∣m′⟩∣2. In the J3​ eigenbasis,
U(y,θ)=(cos(θ/2)sin(θ/2)​−sin(θ/2)cos(θ/2)​).
(76)
The transition from m=1/2 to m′=−1/2 thus has probability sin2(θ/2)=1−cos2(θ/2). A=1,B=−1​.

The asymptotic scattering wavefunction is Ψ∼eikz+f(θ)eikr/r. For a real central potential, the scattering phase shift δl​ multiplies the outgoing component of each partial wave relative to the incoming one by e2iδl​. Matching the incident-wave normalization gives
Ψ∼2ikr1​∑l≥0​(2l+1)[e2iδl​eikr−(−1)le−ikr]Pl​(cosθ).

Subtract the given incident plane wave expansion. Since e2iδl​−1=2ieiδl​sinδl​, the scattering amplitude is
f(θ)=k1​l≥0∑​(2l+1)eiδl​sinδl​Pl​(cosθ)​.

Orthogonality ∫−11​Pl​Pj​dx=2δlj​/(2l+1) eliminates cross terms in σ=∫∣f∣2dΩ, giving σ=(4π/k2)l∑​(2l+1)sin2δl​​.
For the spherical square well, the regular reduced radial l=0 wave is Asin(κr) inside and Bsin(kr+δ0​) outside, with κ2=k2+γ2. Continuity of the wave and its derivative gives the logarithmic-derivative matching relation κcot(κa)=kcot(ka+δ0​), or
katan(ka+δ0​)​=κatan(κa)​.
(79)
At zeros of the denominators the original matching relation supplies the limiting interpretation.
Under the stated deep-well approximation, put x=ka and B0​=tan(γa)/(γa). The condition δ0​∈πZ is tanx/x=B0​. If B0​<0, its first positive solution lies in (π/2,π); if B0​=0, it is π. For 0<B0​≤1, a solution lies in (π,3π/2) because there tanx/x rises continuously from zero to infinity. If B0​>1, the first positive solution lies in (0,π/2), where tanx/x rises from one to infinity. The limiting pole case gives x=π/2 by the cotangent relation. Thus 0<k0​<3π/(2a)​, without calculating the integer phase index. The use of κ≃γ presumes the located wave numbers remain small compared with γ.

35C OurBigBook.com
Each one-particle momentum state occupies volume (2πℏ)3/V in momentum space. Counting the spherical shell gives the density of states
g(ϵ)=2π2ℏ3V​ϵ′(p(ϵ))p(ϵ)2​​.
(80)
The increasing dispersion law permits inversion, and the density is zero below any minimum allowed energy. No additional spin degeneracy is included here.
For noninteracting particles, the classical Boltzmann sum factorizes into zN. Dividing by N! accounts for indistinguishability without quantum exchange corrections, giving the partition function Z=zN/N!, with z=∫g(ϵ)e−ϵ/(kT)dϵ. Differentiation with respect to inverse temperature gives
E=zN​∫0∞​g(ϵ)ϵe−ϵ/(kT)dϵ​.
(81)
Fixed mode indices have momenta proportional to L−1 because the boundary quantization condition fixes pL/ℏ. As V=L3, ∂p/∂V=−p/(3V) and ∂ϵ/∂V=−pϵ′(p)/(3V). The pressure P=kT∂V​logZ, evaluated by differentiating the mode sum, therefore obeys
PV=3zN​∫0∞​g(ϵ)pϵ′(p)e−ϵ/(kT)dϵ​.
(82)
For nonrelativistic particles ϵ=p2/(2m), so PV=2E/3 and E=3NkT/2. For massless relativistic particles ϵ=cp, so PV=E/3 and E=3NkT. Both obey PV=NkT.
The nonrelativistic thermal wavelength is λth​=h/2πmkT​, and z=V/λth3​. If λth​≪(V/N)1/3, then Nλth3​/V≪1: occupation per thermal quantum state is small. Wave packets scarcely overlap and exchange corrections to Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution are negligible, justifying the classical formulas.

Use metric compatibility and the symmetric Levi-Civita connection. Expanding ka​=gac​kc gives
∇b​ka​+∇a​kb​=gac​∂b​kc+gbc​∂a​kc+kc(∂b​gac​+∂a​gbc​−2Γabd​gdc​).
(83)
The Christoffel formula makes the bracket ∂c​gab​. Thus the Killing equation is equivalent to the displayed coordinate formula in the question, also the vanishing Lie derivative of the metric.
Along an affinely parametrized geodesic with tangent V,
Vb∇b​(Vaka​)=ka​Vb∇b​Va+VaVb∇b​ka​=0.
(84)
The first term vanishes by the geodesic equation and the second by the Killing equation, because VaVb is symmetric. This proves the geodesic conserved quantity from a Killing vector.
For ds2=−du2+u2dv2, the three independent coordinate Killing conditions are
∂u​ku=0,uku+u2∂v​kv=0,−∂v​ku+u2∂u​kv=0.
(85)
The field (0,1) satisfies all three immediately. For e−v(1,u−1), the second equation reads ue−v−ue−v=0, and the third reads e−v−e−v=0. For ev(−1,u−1), they read −uev+uev=0 and ev−ev=0. The first equation holds for both, verifying all three Killing vector fields.
Their conserved contractions with (u˙,v˙) may be denoted
γ=u2v˙,α=e−v(−u˙+uv˙),β=ev(u˙+uv˙).
(86)
Adding the last two expressions after multiplying by ev,e−v gives
αev+βe−v=2γ/u​.
(87)
To identify these loci, set T=ucoshv, X=usinhv. The metric becomes −dT2+dX2, and the equation becomes (α+β)T+(α−β)X=2γ, a straight line in Minkowski spacetime. Nontrivial such lines, parametrized affinely, are exactly the geodesics in this coordinate patch. The all-zero choice of constants is a vacuous equation rather than an individual geodesic.

The lubrication approximation applies in a gap thin compared with its horizontal scale, with small slopes, no slip at the walls, negligible inertia, and approximately constant pressure across the gap. Continuity makes the horizontal velocity much larger than the normal velocity. At t=0, write h(x)=h0​+δx/L, where δ=Δh and ∣δ∣<h0​ keeps the gap open.
The horizontal Stokes equation becomes μuyy​=px​. Both plates have zero horizontal velocity, so
u=2μpx​​y(y−h),Q(x)=∫0h​udy=−12μh3​px​​.
(88)
Integrated incompressibility with the moving upper wall gives ht​+Qx​=0. Since ht​=−V, Qx​=V, and Q(x)=Vx+C, giving Q(L)−Q(−L)=2VL.
Equal end pressures impose ∫−LL​(Vx+C)/h3dx=0. The two elementary integrals are
∫−LL​h3dx​=(h02​−δ2)22Lh0​​,∫−LL​h3xdx​=−(h02​−δ2)22L2δ​.
(89)
Hence C=VLδ/h0​. In endpoint form this pressure condition is (h0​−δ)Q(L)+(h0​+δ)Q(−L)=0. Combining it with the flux difference gives
Q(±L)=VL(δ/h0​±1)​.
(90)
The limits δ=0 recover equal outward fluxes.
The horizontal velocity scale is U∼VL/h0​. The ratio of convective inertia ρU2/L to viscous force μU/h02​ is ρVh0​/μ; the unsteady term on time scale h0​/V has the same ratio. Therefore, alongside h0​/L≪1, the required condition is V≪μ/(ρh0​)​.

For the Rayleigh wave, take displacement potentials in the x,z plane,
ux​=ϕx​−ψz​,uz​=ϕz​+ψx​,ϕ=Aekαzeik(x−ct),ψ=Bekβzeik(x−ct),

The radix-two Fast Fourier transform recursively splits the input into even and odd subsequences until length one, then assembles the transforms using the FFT butterfly identities. For n=8, the recursive leaf order is the bit-reversed order y0​,y4​,y2​,y6​,y1​,y5​,y3​,y7​. The three assembly stages have block sizes two, four and eight. In a block of size q, butterfly number ℓ maps (a,b) to (a+ωqℓ​b,a−ωqℓ​b).
